catalog_quote: [p.25] Mikasuki has a pitch accent prosodic system, i.e. contrastive pitch is found only on certain key syllables in a word. Nonkey syllables have noncontrastive pitch (Haas 1977:1). There are three contrastive pitches-- low /`/, mid /¯/, and high /´/-- the distribution of which is determined morphologically. ... [p.27] there are certain obligatory stress patterns in Mikasuki. A word may have only one stressed syllable and this stressed syllable will have either /mid/ or /high/ pitch. Specific grammatical restrictions operate on stress, as in the case of the imperative suffix, which must be stressed. ... changes in the location of the stressed syllable alter an adjective to form the comparative and superlative. ... there are certain typical distributional patterns of stress according to the root class of the word. tone_statements.citation: Derrick-Mescua, Mary Tyler. 1980. A Phonology and Morphology of Mikasuki. PhD dissertation, University of Florida. xvi+473 pp. Ann Arbor: UMI.
tone_statements.quote: The prosodic system of Mikasuki is the pitch-accent type, in which contrastive pitch is found on specified syllables in a word. Syllables which take one of the three contrastive pitches, high ///, mid /-/, or low /\ /, are called key syllables. Non-key syllables are those for which pitch is non-contrastive (Haas, 1977:1). The occurrence of key syllables is governed by morphological class. Noun roots contain only key syllables, and uninflected verb roots contain no key syllables.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: all quoted passages found verbatim on the page scan we hold at the stated dissertation pages 25, 27, 28 (archive.org leaves 33, 35, 36); locator and 'page-image' grade are accurate; an independent the compilers (2026-09-12) had already re-confirmed the same pages. (2) Deciding source: a 1982 primary fieldwork-based PhD grammar (193 pp) whose prosody section is explicit and internally consistent: contrastive low/mid/high pitch on morphologically determined key syllables, one stressed syllable per word always carrying mid/high pitch, stress location in verbs part of tense/aspect marking, noun stress non-contrastive and tied to pitch. That supports classification tonal (pitch accent) with morphology as the placement mechanism; no weight- or count-computable stress rule exists in the source (p.26 weight constrains pitch and verb shape, not stress position).
